strengths: Clear conceptual framing that connects prompt-tuning/neologism techniques with the skill-composition formalism of Arora & Goyal (2023), yielding a coherent problem statement (P1-P3) and a principled way to evaluate compositional generalization via ID/OOD skill splits.

The preliminary XOR/XNOR experiment across four open-source LLMs is a nice, low-cost piece of evidence motivating the core hypothesis that vocabulary tokens can encode procedural knowledge, and the XOR vs. XNOR frequency contrast is a clever natural control.

The main experiments use a well-controlled synthetic testbed with explicit sample-skill mappings, enabling clean measurement of compositional transfer (P2) and zero-shot multi-skill composition (P3); Skill Neologisms consistently outperform LoRA and Prompt Tuning baselines under matched trainable-parameter budgets.

Thorough ablations (token length, training composition complexity, initialization) provide some mechanistic insight into why skill neologisms generalize better than the baselines (e.g., limited capacity as inductive bias).
Extensive appendix with hyperparameters, dataset construction, and compute details supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: All core skill-neologism experiments (Section 5) use a single very small model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) on a purely synthetic digit-transformation task; there is no evidence that the method scales to modern-size LLMs or to natural-language skills, which substantially limits the significance of the central claims relative to the paper's broad motivating narrative about 'ever-growing range of skills' in modern LLMs.

Only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) and seven pretrained skills are tested; the skill space is narrow and the operations are simple deterministic digit transforms, so it is unclear whether findings generalize to more complex, less rule-like procedural skills (e.g., reasoning, coding).

Absolute OOD accuracies remain modest (roughly 0.57-0.85 depending on setting), and multi-skill zero-shot composition (Figure 5) degrades substantially with sequence length, so the method is shown to be 'better than baselines' rather than convincingly 'solving' the stated problem.

The practical recipe for constructing skill-centered datasets for real-world skills is only sketched qualitatively (via LLM annotation or curated multi-labels) and is not empirically validated anywhere in the paper; this is a central practical requirement of the method but remains unverified.

No large/frontier LLM is used to validate that learned skill neologisms (as opposed to the pre-existing 'XOR' style tokens) actually work in realistic settings; the gap between the toy experiments and the motivating claims about modern LLMs is not bridged.

Statistical rigor is somewhat limited: it is unclear how many random seeds were used per configuration beyond averaging across held-out skills, and no significance tests are reported for the comparisons between Skill Neologisms and baselines.

strengths: The paper introduces a conceptually interesting combination of vocabulary-level neologisms (Hewitt et al., 2025) with skill-centered training data, and clearly articulates a useful taxonomy of properties (P1-P3) that any skill-based continual learning method should satisfy.

The synthetic digit-sequence benchmark is well-designed for isolating compositional generalization: exact skill labels, controllable ID/OOD splits over both skill combinations and sequence lengths, and clean comparisons against LoRA and Prompt Tuning baselines under matched parameter budgets.

The ablations (skill token length, training composition complexity, initialization) are informative and reveal a plausible inductive-bias mechanism (limited capacity favoring composable rather than overfit representations).
Extensive appendices provide hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset construction details that would aid reproducibility of the reported synthetic experiments.
The limitations section is candid, explicitly acknowledging the proof-of-concept nature of the work, the computational cost issue, and dependence on skill-centered dataset availability.
weaknesses: The central claim that skill neologisms provide a "scalable path towards skill-based continual learning" for LLMs is not actually supported by the evidence: all core experiments (Section 5) use a single 0.5B-parameter model on a narrow synthetic algorithmic task with only 9 total operations, and only two new skills (SHIFT, INV-POL) are ever learned. This is far too small and artificial a setting to support claims about "modern LLMs" and general skill-based continual learning.

The paper's own limitations admit that training skill neologisms requires full backpropagation through the model at cost comparable to fine-tuning, directly undermining the advertised "scalability" of the approach relative to alternatives — this is a serious tension between the framing/abstract and the acknowledged practical constraints.

The motivating XOR/XNOR experiment (Section 4) is weak evidence for the core hypothesis: N=100 samples, 3-bit inputs (a tiny, easily pattern-matched space), and a single frequency-based confound (XOR vs XNOR corpus frequency) is not sufficient to establish that vocabulary tokens generically "encapsulate procedural knowledge" as opposed to simply serving as task-identifying labels that trigger memorized behavior — an alternative explanation not ruled out.

Key comparative claims are under-explained mechanistically: the paper observes that Prompt Tuning underperforms Skill Neologisms with the same number of trainable parameters, but the explanation offered ("semantically embedding the soft tokens inside prompts may provide additional flexibility") is speculative and not tested via any additional experiment (e.g., ablating the insertion function, probing embeddings, or varying where tokens are placed for PT).

No experiments are run in natural language or realistic instruction-tuning settings despite the paper explicitly proposing (and citing feasibility for) constructing skill-centered datasets via LLM metacognitive labeling; this leaves the practical applicability of the method to real skills entirely untested, weakening the significance of the contribution.

Variance in results is often large relative to effect sizes (e.g., Table 5/6 show std as large as the mean in several cells), and the number of held-out skill conditions (6) is small, making some reported trends (e.g., composition complexity improving OOD performance) statistically fragile.

The comparison set of baselines is limited to vanilla LoRA and vanilla Prompt Tuning; the related-work section itself cites several more sophisticated prefix-transfer methods (SPoT, ATTEMPT, Multitask Prompt Tuning) explicitly designed to improve OOD transferability, none of which are empirically compared against, despite being the most directly relevant competing approaches for Property 2.

strengths: The paper introduces a clear and well-motivated formalism (skill neologisms) that operationalizes three concrete desiderata (P1-P3) for skill-based continual learning, building coherently on the Arora & Goyal skill-composition framework.

The motivating experiment in Section 4 (XOR vs. XNOR keyword vs. description across four open-source LLMs) is a nice, low-cost piece of evidence supporting the core hypothesis that vocabulary tokens can encode procedural knowledge, and it is a good narrative bridge to the main method.

The controlled synthetic experiments cleanly isolate ID vs. OOD skill composition and enable rigorous comparison against LoRA and Prompt Tuning under matched training budgets/soft-token counts, showing a consistent ordering (Skill Neologisms > Prompt Tuning > LoRA) on OOD composition (Figure 4, Figure A2).

Zero-shot multi-skill composition (Property 3) is demonstrated against a sensible in-context learning baseline across multiple sequence lengths, and the result (skill neologisms > ICL) is a meaningful qualitative finding.

The ablation studies (token capacity, training composition complexity, initialization) are thoughtful and produce an interesting non-monotonic capacity-generalization trade-off, adding some mechanistic insight beyond the headline results.

The appendix is unusually thorough (full hyperparameters, dataset construction, per-skill breakdowns), aiding reproducibility, and the limitations section is candid about scope, computational cost, and dataset-construction challenges.
weaknesses: All core method experiments (Section 5) use a single, very small base model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) fine-tuned via LoRA on a synthetic digit-sequence task with a handful of explicitly-labeled operations; it is unclear whether findings transfer to genuinely pretrained LLM skills, natural-language settings, or larger models, which substantially limits the significance of the claims relative to the broad framing of the paper ("towards skill-based continual learning").

The skill inventory is very small (7 pretrained skills, 2 new skills), and the insertion function in the main experiments is a trivial token swap; this is a much simpler setting than the implicit, entangled skills the introduction motivates the work with, so the proof-of-concept nature is not just a stated limitation but a real constraint on how much can be concluded.

Many reported results have large variance across held-out skills (e.g., Table 5: INV-POL kmax=1 C2 = .36±.44; Table A2: INV-POL random init C2(SUB)=.00 while others are ~.8-.9), suggesting the averaged headline numbers can mask highly unstable, skill-dependent behavior that is not sufficiently discussed or explained.

There is no full fine-tuning baseline in the compositional transfer experiments to contextualize how much OOD generalization gap remains between skill neologisms and an upper-bound method, despite fine-tuning being prominently discussed as a comparator in the introduction and Table 1.

Table 1's claim that prefix-based methods can achieve P2 ("*Achievable with skill-centered training") is only partially supported by the paper's own results — Prompt Tuning trained with the same skill-centered data still substantially underperforms Skill Neologisms on OOD composition (Figure 4), so the asterisked claim reads as more optimistic than the evidence shown.

The skill-token-length ablation (Figure 6), which produces one of the more novel mechanistic claims (capacity as inductive bias), is run with only a single fixed held-out skill (ADD) rather than averaged across the six held-out skills used elsewhere, weakening confidence in the generality of the capacity/generalization trade-off.

The construction of skill-centered datasets — acknowledged as a key requirement — is only sketched at a high level (e.g., relying on LLM metacognition or curated multi-labels) without any experiment demonstrating this works in a less synthetic setting, leaving the practical scalability of the approach largely untested.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framing of 'skill neologisms' combining vocabulary-level soft tokens with skill-centered training data, clearly distinguished from prior prompt-tuning/prefix-tuning approaches via a crisp three-property taxonomy (no weight updates, compositional transfer, multi-skill composition).

The motivating XOR/XNOR experiment in Section 4 is a clever and simple demonstration that pretrained token embeddings already encode procedural knowledge asymmetrically based on pretraining frequency, providing a nice conceptual bridge to the main proposal.

The controlled synthetic digit-sequence task is well designed, with explicit skill definitions and clean ID/OOD splits, enabling precise measurement of compositional transfer (P2) and zero-shot multi-skill composition (P3) against LoRA and prompt tuning baselines.

Thorough ablation studies (skill token length, training composition complexity, initialization strategy, label noise robustness) that meaningfully probe the mechanisms behind why skill neologisms generalize better than LoRA/prompt tuning.
Extension to the more realistic Skill-Mix natural language benchmark strengthens external validity of the claims beyond the synthetic setting.
Strong reproducibility support: extensive appendix with hyperparameters, dataset construction details, prompts, and computational resource specifications.
weaknesses: Experiments rely on a very small base model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) for the main controlled study and a modest 3B model for the Skill-Mix validation; it is unclear whether findings (especially the inductive-bias-from-limited-capacity argument) hold at the scale of frontier LLMs where skill neologisms would be most useful.

The natural language validation (Section 6) is a single case study with only two target skills on one model, N=50 test queries, and grading performed by a single LLM judge (GPT-5) without human verification or inter-rater reliability checks—this limits confidence in the generalizability of the zero-shot composition claim to realistic settings.

Zero-shot multi-skill composition accuracy in the synthetic setting (Figure 5) decays substantially with sequence length (dropping toward ~0.2), and the OOD compositional-transfer results (Figure 4) show very high variance across held-out skills (e.g., prompt tuning near-zero for some Sheld-out but comparable to skill neologisms for others), suggesting the improvement over baselines may be less robust/consistent than the aggregated averages imply.

The claimed computational efficiency advantage is undercut by the paper's own admission that training still requires full backpropagation through the frozen model, making costs comparable to fine-tuning in practice—this tempers the practical scalability argument central to the paper's motivation.

Baselines are limited to LoRA and standard prompt tuning; other relevant continual/compositional learning approaches (e.g., in-context skill descriptions as in Skill-in-Context, multitask prompt tuning transfer methods like SPoT/ATTEMPT discussed in related work) are not empirically compared despite being closely related.

The synthetic digit-operation skills are quite simple and homogeneous (arithmetic/permutation operations on digit strings), and it remains unclear how the approach would scale to a larger, more heterogeneous skill inventory or to skills requiring richer reasoning, which is acknowledged only briefly in the limitations.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and timely problem (extending LLM capabilities without catastrophic forgetting) and clearly articulates three desiderata (P1-P3) that provide a useful comparative framework against fine-tuning, LoRA, and prompt tuning.

The controlled synthetic digit-sequence task is a reasonable testbed: it allows exact construction of ID/OOD skill splits and clean measurement of compositional transfer, which is hard to do in natural language settings.

The ablation studies (token length, composition complexity in training data, initialization, label noise) provide some mechanistic insight into why skill neologisms might generalize better than LoRA, namely the inductive bias from limited capacity and skill-centered training.

The idea of combining vocabulary-level soft tokens (neologisms) with skill-centered datasets to get zero-shot composability is a reasonably novel combination of existing ingredients (Hewitt et al. neologisms + skill-centric data construction), and the related work discussion is thorough.
weaknesses: The central claims about 'scalable' skill-based continual learning are never actually tested at scale: all controlled experiments use a 0.5B parameter model with only 2 new skills, and the natural-language validation uses a single 3B model with exactly 2 target skills (modus ponens, statistical syllogism) and N=300 training samples, 50 test queries. This is far too small to support claims of scalability or wide applicability to realistic settings.

Multi-skill composition (Property 3) is only ever demonstrated with exactly two independently trained skills, never three or more; whether skill neologisms compose gracefully (or degrade) when more skills are stacked together is left entirely untested, which undermines the 'continual learning' framing where many skills should accumulate over time.

The Skill-Mix evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (GPT-5) with no human validation of grading quality, no inter-rater reliability check, and no report of multiple seeds/runs, making the headline natural-language result (Figure 7) fragile and hard to trust given it is the paper's only real-world evidence.

Baseline comparisons (LoRA, prompt tuning) are not clearly tuned to be competitive—e.g., LoRA rank, learning rates, and epochs appear fixed rather than swept, and prompt tuning/skill neologisms share identical hyperparameters without justification that this is a fair point of comparison for each method's optimal regime.

Results show very high variance across held-out skills (e.g., Table A1/A2 standard deviations often comparable to or larger than the differences being claimed, such as INV-POL OOD accuracy swinging from .00 to .91 across held-out skills), yet the paper reports only averages in the main text, obscuring how unreliable the composability claim is for individual skill pairs.

The motivating experiment in Section 4 (XOR vs. XNOR keyword effect) is a single anecdotal skill pair across 4 models with no broader survey of which tokens act as 'skill tokens' and why, so it provides weak empirical support for the paper's foundational premise that pretrained vocabulary already encodes procedural knowledge.

The REV skill is quietly excluded from held-out skills due to overfitting/non-generalization during base-model pretraining (Appendix A.1), but this failure case and its implications for the generality of the approach are not meaningfully discussed in the main text.

The insertion function ϕ_S, which determines how skill tokens are inserted into text, is manually crafted per setting and is critical to the method's success, yet there is no systematic study of its effect or robustness, which weakens the method's claimed general applicability and reproducibility in new domains.

Practical construction of skill-centered datasets for less structured domains is acknowledged as a limitation but never empirically demonstrated beyond synthetic data and a narrowly curated two-skill Skill-Mix subset, leaving the core scalability claim largely speculative.

No comparison is made against alternative parameter-efficient continual learning baselines beyond vanilla LoRA/prompt tuning (e.g., modular adapter merging, mixture-of-experts style routing, or other composable PEFT methods), limiting the significance of the contribution relative to the broader continual-learning literature.

strengths: The core idea—combining prompt-tuning-style soft tokens with skill-centered (rather than task-centered) training data, integrated as new vocabulary items—is a clean and original synthesis that directly targets two properties (OOD compositional transfer and zero-shot multi-skill composition) that existing PEFT/ICL approaches structurally cannot achieve.

The motivating experiment in Section 4 (XOR vs. XNOR token behavior across four open-source LLMs) is a nice, low-cost piece of evidence that pretrained vocabulary already encodes procedural/skill-like knowledge, providing good intuition for why vocabulary-level intervention is a sensible lever.

The controlled synthetic digit-sequence benchmark is well designed: it has explicit, unambiguous skill labels, clean ID/OOD skill splits via leave-one-skill-out, and permutation-robust test set construction, which allows a precise test of Properties 2 and 3 that would be hard to obtain in natural language settings.

The head-to-head comparison against LoRA and prompt tuning on OOD composition (Figure 4) and against in-context learning on multi-skill composition (Figure 5) is informative and shows a clear, consistent advantage for skill neologisms, not just on average but across most held-out skill conditions.

The ablation suite (token capacity, training composition complexity, initialization, label noise) gives useful mechanistic insight into why skill neologisms work (e.g., limited capacity as an inductive bias against overfitting to the training composition), going beyond a pure existence-proof result.

The Skill-Mix extension, while limited, demonstrates that the core zero-shot composition claim (P3) is not an artifact of the synthetic task alone and partially transfers to an instruction-tuned LLM and natural-language skills.

The paper is transparent about limitations (dataset construction difficulty, soft-token sensitivity, compute cost comparable to fine-tuning) and provides extensive reproducibility details in the appendix (hyperparameters, prompts, dataset construction).
weaknesses: All controlled experiments use a very small base model (Qwen2.5-0.5B) and a narrow set of 7 synthetic digit operations; it is unclear whether the composability advantages persist at the scale and skill diversity relevant to real deployment, which weakens the significance of the claimed path toward "scalable" continual learning.

The natural language validation (Section 6) is quite thin: only two target skills, N=300 training samples, 50 test queries, a single 3B model, and apparently single-run results with no reported variance across seeds—this is a much weaker evidentiary base than the synthetic experiments and is insufficient to strongly support generalization claims to realistic settings.
Grading on Skill-Mix relies solely on GPT-5 as an automatic judge with no human verification or inter-rater reliability check, which introduces potential judge bias/noise that is not quantified.

The central practical requirement—construction of skill-centered datasets—is acknowledged as a key bottleneck but is not seriously addressed or empirically stress-tested beyond the synthetic setting and one small hand-curated natural-language example; the proposed solutions (LLM metacognitive annotation, curated multi-label datasets) are mentioned but never actually used or validated in experiments.

Several ablation results (Tables 5, 6, A1, A2) show large standard deviations relative to the differences being discussed (e.g., averaged over only 6 held-out skills), yet are used to draw fairly strong qualitative conclusions (e.g., about composition complexity or initialization effects) without statistical testing.

The comparison baselines are limited to LoRA, prompt tuning, and plain ICL; other relevant modular/continual-learning baselines (e.g., adapter mixtures, model merging, retrieval-augmented skill libraries) are not empirically compared, making it harder to judge the method's relative significance against the broader continual-learning literature.

The paper's claims in the abstract/conclusion ("scalable path towards skill-based continual learning") somewhat outpace the evidence, which is restricted to two new skills composed pairwise in both settings; it remains untested whether neologisms scale to many (e.g., dozens) of incrementally added skills without interference or embedding-space crowding.
